catalog_quote: 2.3 Suprasegmentals Nkonya has high and low tones which contrast, with tonal sandhi producing multiple phonetic tone levels. See section 6 for details. The contrast between high and low tones is illustrated by the minimal pair [-fa] ‘shelter for yams’ and [-fa] ‘grass’. I have indicated high tone with [a], low tone with [a], high falling tone ... [p.29:] 6.1 Introduction The analysis of tone in this section is rather cursory. Nevertheless, a few comments on the tonal characteristics of Nkonya are necessary. Nkonya, like other Tano languages (specifically Akan), is a two tone language with contrast between Low (L) and High (H) tones. It also shares with them the phenomenon of downstep, although there are some significant differences in the exact manifestation of the phenomenon. Nkonya also shares with other Tano languages the phenomenon of High tone spread. Unique to Nkonya is the lowering of H tones. That is, under certain conditions some H tones are lowered to the same level as that of a L tone.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkonya is described as a two-tone (H/L) terrace-level tone language with downstep, H spread and H lowering; the only modern primary phonology has a 'Suprasegmentals' section that covers tone alone and makes no statement of any kind about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement). Tone-related: word-final glottal stop before pause interacts with tone; noun-class prefixes are L.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described for words in isolation and in phrases (pitch traces of sentences); no word- or phrase-level stress/accent statement anywhere in the source.
new_statements.identity_note: Peacock 2007 covers both Nkonya dialects (Northern, Wurupong northward; Southern, Tepo southward), with most data from Wurupong (Northern); Reineke 1972 and Stewart 1966 document the Southern dialect only. Westermann's 'Guang in Togo' (1922) and 'Landschaft Nkunya' (1932) = Nkonya (nkon1248), spelled Nkunya.

new_statements.quote: Die Töne. 9. Es sind die gleichen Töne zu unterscheiden wie im Ewe, auch die Bezeichnung der Töne ist dieselbe wie dort; s. Grammatik der Ewe-Sprache 5; — mit dem Unterschiede jedoch, daß Wörter ohne Tonzeichen nicht als tieftonig, sondern eben als unbezeichnet anzusehen sind [...]. Auch nasale Konsonanten und l können ihren eigenen Ton haben [...]. Wie im Ewe hat auch jedes Zw seinen eigenen Ton, aber dieser bleibt nicht wie dort in der Konjugation unverändert, sondern das rein etymologische Tonsystem wird überkreuzt durch das grammatische, d.h. durch die Verwendung der Töne zur Bildung der Verbalformen.
new_statements.translation: The tones. 9. The same tones are to be distinguished as in Ewe, and the notation of the tones is the same as there (see Grammatik der Ewe-Sprache par. 5) -- with the difference, however, that words without tone marks are not to be taken as low-toned but simply as unmarked [...]. Nasal consonants and l can also carry their own tone [...]. As in Ewe every verb has its own tone, but it does not stay unchanged in conjugation as it does there; rather the purely etymological tone system is cross-cut by the grammatical one, i.e. by the use of the tones to form the verbal forms.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Peacock 2007: Nkonya tonal, H/L contrast, no stress statement). Westermann 1922 likewise describes the Nkunya-based Guang as tonal (Ewe-type tone marking, lexical + grammatical verb tone) and makes no stress/accent statement for it; it adds only historical detail (more marked tone levels: Hoch/Tief/Mittel/Hochtief/Tiefhoch in the notation, grammatical tone in the verb). The bib_tag 'likely states stress' is not borne out for the Guang chapter: the book's stress remarks concern Ahlo, Akasele and Bargu, not Guang/Nkonya.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Guang (described from the Nkunya = Nkonya dialect of the informant Andreas Anno) is treated as a tone language with the Ewe tone inventory (high, low, mid, high-low, low-high marks per the Vorwort pp.2-3), lexical tone on every verb overlaid by grammatical tone in conjugation, and recurrent noun tone patterns (par. 10: e.g. sg. low-low vs pl. high + high-low). Nothing is said about word stress, accent or a 'Starkton' for Guang; Westermann uses such terms only in the Ahlo (p.18 'dynamischer Akzent'), Akasele (p.66) and Bargu (p.127 'Starkton.. auf der Stammsilbe') chapters of the same book.
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone only: par. 10 notes frequent tone patterns, e.g. prefixless disyllabic nouns low-low in the singular, high + high-low in the plural: sera - asapa 'python', kpasi - akpasi 'rat')
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Guang' grammatical introduction and dictionary are explicitly based on the speech of one informant, Andreas Anno from Nkunya (= Nkonya, east bank of the Volta; recorded Berlin 1913-14; pp.147, 151-152), with forms from other Guang dialects (Late, Kyerepong, Anum, Boso, Nkemi, Kratschi, Nawuri, Salaga, Obutu, Simpa, Anyanga) cited only where they differ; the tone paragraphs 9-10 therefore describe Nkonya (nkon1248).
